title: A recovery design is a structure that allows operations to resume after a failure.
body: Recovery design does not assume that errors will never occur; rather, it is an approach that allows users to resume their tasks in the event of a failure. “Fallback” refers to an alternative path, “retry” means to try again, and “safe default” refers to a default value that is not risky when the actual value is unknown. Common issues, such as network failures or JSON parsing errors, should be addressed in the design alongside UI guidance, logs, retry buttons, and cached data. When reading code, evaluate whether it hides failures, explains them, or leads to a recovery action. Being “publicly available” is not the same as being “commercially reusable,” and the ability to modify the data and the requirement to attribute the source must also be considered separately. When dealing with public data, open licenses, derived data, and source ratings, you must save both the original URL and the usage policy. In learning apps or submitted materials, credibility is built not only on data quality but also on managing evidence that can be explained later. title: Asynchrony and concurrency are structures that determine how to divide up tasks that involve waiting.
body: Asynchronous code is a structure that allows other tasks to proceed while waiting, rather than pausing to process long-running tasks sequentially. `async` and `await` are indicators of asynchronous flow, while `gather` is a pattern for waiting for multiple tasks simultaneously. Semaphores and rate limits are mechanisms that prevent too many tasks from running at the same time. When reading code, you must distinguish whether it is designed to speed up actual computations or to reduce waiting times for network or file operations. detail: Refactoring is the process of making code easier to read and modify while preserving its functionality. We’ll look at removing duplication, naming conventions, separating configuration, using smaller functions, and backward compatibility. Maintainability is a criterion that asks whether code that’s currently running will remain safe after the next modification. Therefore, patches that change the structure without verifying the results are risky.

title: System concepts are understood by comparing the differences in roles, such as sensors, processes, and ontologies.
body: The System Concepts card goes beyond Python syntax to cover the background knowledge needed to understand real-world systems. Sensors observe values, actuators generate actions, and controllers make decisions based on inputs. Noise, drift, and synchronization illustrate the reality that data is not always clean or received simultaneously. Ontology, OWL, SHACL, and SPARQL are ways of structuring knowledge and relationships. Rather than memorizing these cards, readers should study them by comparing the different roles each term plays within a system. When reviewing these cards, learners should not view “reading system concepts by comparing role differences, such as sensors, processes, and ontologies” as a single overarching theme; instead, they should first identify what role each concept plays in the code or concepts of the current problem. When reading, compare the differences in roles, such as those of sensors, actuators, and controllers. Words like “thread,” “process,” “async,” “ontology,” “SHACL,” and “SPARQL” are also easier to understand when you look at their positions within the system rather than trying to memorize them. If related lessons are grouped broadly, don’t try to memorize all the concepts at once; instead, select just one or two key terms from the current card and connect their causes and effects. Review these together using the comparison cards for sensors/actuators/controllers, noise/drift/sync, OWL/SHACL/SPARQL, and threads/processes. Finally, use this topic as supplementary material in the “Practical Python Reading” section to connect code snippets, data structures, user flows, and validation criteria.
when_to_show: Let's look at them together on the comparison cards for sensors/actuators/controllers, noise/drift/sync, OWL/SHACL/SPARQL, and threads/processes.
detail: When learning system concepts, it’s better to understand them by comparing the roles each element plays within the system rather than simply memorizing the terms. Terms such as “thread,” “process,” “async,” and “ontology” are also best understood in terms of their position and role.

title: Other runtime product patterns attempt to connect features to user flows
body: The "Other Runtime Product Patterns" card is a supplementary card designed to group together runtime product features—such as Notes, Search, Progress, Save, Performance, and UI Feedback—that are not broken down into separate sub-cards. When reviewing these cards, focus on following the user’s flow—opening the app, entering values, checking results, and moving on to the next action—rather than memorizing specific technical terms. Runtime features relate to how the state changes, the screen updates, and data is saved while the code is executing. Therefore, instead of focusing on a single function or file, you should examine input, state changes, saving, recovery, display, and validation criteria together. This card is not intended to broaden the scope; rather, it serves as a final fallback card that safely connects the remaining product flows that do not fit into separate subcards. When related lessons are linked to this card, start by selecting just one or two key concepts from the current card. Then, trace them step by step to see what screen changes or saved results those concepts produce for the user, what recovery paths exist in case of failure, and under what conditions they can be verified through testing or validation. If a concept seems too broad, prioritize reading more specific subcards from the “notes,” “search,” “progress,” “storage,” “performance,” or “UI feedback” categories. A9_BODY_THICKENED: This card is no longer intended to cover all broad runtime features; rather, it serves as a fallback card that handles only the remaining product flows that have not been broken down into detailed subcards. Therefore, if you see clear subtopics such as notes, search, progress, storage, performance, or UI feedback, it’s best to read the respective A9 detail cards first. If this card is linked, identify where the key terms of the current lesson appear in the user flow. For example, you can examine the sequence of events: what values are entered, what states change, and what screens or saved results follow. Finally, rather than memorizing a list of features, think of runtime product patterns as the interconnected structure that enables users to reopen the app and continue learning.
when_to_show: View user notes, search filters, saved settings, progress backups, performance metrics, and dashboard cards all in one place.
detail: A runtime product pattern is a card that connects the flow of a user opening an app, entering values, experiencing state changes, viewing results, and continuing from there. Since it serves as a fallback for product features that are not broken down into separate detail cards, it allows you to review input, state changes, saving, recovery, display, and validation criteria all at once.

title: Notes and bookmarks are features that allow learners to mark where they left off.
body: The note and bookmark features are runtime functions that allow users to revisit important cards or confusing concepts later. When terms such as “bookmark,” “favorite,” “user note,” “note editor,” and “auto-save note” appear, they should be viewed not as simple save buttons, but as mechanisms that help users retain what they’ve learned. A well-implemented system reliably links card IDs to user input, restores data after a refresh, and distinguishes between empty notes and deleted notes. From a privacy perspective, since user-written notes may be sensitive, they must be kept separate from analytics events. When reading the code, examine the save key, load order, auto-save timing, and the filter and export flows together. Think of this card as serving the role of connecting “where I left off” and “what I need to review” when the learner reopens the app. A9_BODY_THICKENED: When reviewing the code for notes and bookmarks, first verify the save targets and restoration points. The key points are which cards the user has marked, how those marks are linked to the card IDs, and whether they reappear after refreshing the app. Since user notes are text written directly by the user, they must be separated from analytics events, and care must be taken to ensure that personal notes are not transmitted externally. If auto-save is enabled, verify whether it saves upon each input, after a set period of time, and how it distinguishes between an empty string and deletion. When integrating with search or filters, consider workflows that allow users to view only bookmarked cards or find only cards with notes. The purpose of this feature is to ensure users can return to the app without losing important content.

detail: Notes and bookmarks are features that allow users to return to important cards or concepts they’re unsure about. Check the save key, card ID linking, auto-save timing, the distinction between deleted and empty notes, and restoration after refreshing. Since personal notes can be sensitive, it’s safer to separate them from analytics events. If linked to search and filter functions, review the entire process of retrieving information as well.

title: As the number of cards increases, search, filter, and sort features help you find a learning path.
body: Search, filtering, and sorting are features that help users quickly find the learning items they need as the number of cards increases. When terms such as “keyword search,” “tag filter,” “query string,” “sorting,” and “candidate ranking” appear, they should be interpreted as a process of narrowing down the results based on specific criteria and organizing them in a specific order, rather than displaying the entire dataset. Search compares the input term with the card text; filters use structured values such as tags, levels, and statuses; and sorting applies criteria such as “most recent” or “by difficulty.” By saving conditions in a URL query or local state, users can reopen the same results. When reviewing code, check for input normalization, handling of empty results, filter combinations, performance, and whether there are indicators that help users understand the current conditions. A9_BODY_THICKENED: When reviewing search, filter, and sorting code, start by examining how user input is transformed into specific conditions. Search typically involves normalizing text and comparing it to card titles, descriptions, and concept tags. Filters narrow down the results based on structured values such as level, tag, completion status, and bookmark status. Sorting determines the order in which items are displayed within a given set of results. When multiple conditions are present, the results vary significantly depending on whether they are combined using “AND” or “OR.” An empty state is required when no results are found, and the current page number or scroll position may need to be reset when conditions are changed. As the number of cards increases, this code serves as a guide for learners to find the content they need.
when_to_show: You can view runtime product features, user status, search and filters, notes, progress, performance, and UI feedback all together on a single card.
detail: Search, filter, and sort are features that help users find the learning paths they need as the number of cards increases. Check the following: search term normalization, tag and level filters, AND/OR conditions, sort criteria, handling of empty results, and display of current conditions. When conditions change, the page layout and scroll position may also adjust accordingly. Prompts displayed when no results are found are also important for maintaining the learning flow.

title: Progress, Scores, and Dashboards Should Guide Learners Toward Their Next Steps
body: A progress tracker and dashboard are ineffective if they merely show how much a user has reviewed. When terms like “progress tracking,” “mastery score,” “wrong answer log,” “mistake note,” and “export progress” appear, you’re looking at a system that links that data to the next review action. Learning status is broken down into various indicators, such as the number of completed items, accuracy rate, weak concepts, recent incorrect answers, and number of attempts. A good dashboard suggests which cards to review next or easy review paths rather than simply displaying a lot of numbers. The export feature is useful for backups, submissions, and switching devices, but since it may contain personal learning records, its scope must be clearly defined. When reading the code, verify the storage schema, aggregation criteria, display locations, backup formats, and boundaries of personal information. A9_BODY_THICKENED: When reading code related to progress, scores, and dashboards, distinguish between raw records and aggregated results. Raw records are closer to individual events—such as which problems a user solved, when, and whether they were correct—while aggregated results are summarized information, such as accuracy rates, number of completions, weak concepts, and cards requiring review. A good dashboard doesn’t just stop at displaying numbers; it leads to the next action. For example, it can re-display concepts with many incorrect answers, show the number of cards remaining for today’s goal, or recommend cards that haven’t been reviewed in a while. If an export function is available, it may include personal learning records, so you should verify the scope and format of the export. This card serves as a bridge that helps users understand their learning status and move on to the next review session.
when_to_show: You can view runtime product features, user status, search and filters, notes, progress, performance, and UI feedback all together on a single card.
detail: Progress, Scores, and the Dashboard are features that aggregate original learning records and translate them into the next review action. They categorize data into the number of completed items, accuracy rates, weak concepts, recent incorrect answers, and cards indicating the need for review. Rather than simply displaying a lot of numbers, it’s important to provide a flow that tells users exactly what they need to review right now. The export feature must also specify the scope of the individual’s learning history.

title: Saving and restoring state keeps the user's workflow uninterrupted.
body: Runtime saving and state restoration are features that allow users to continue where they left off even after refreshing or reopening the app. When terms such as `localStorage`, `auto save`, `debounce`, `state restore`, `settings`, and `user data` come up, examine how the screen state is linked to the saved data. Auto-save minimizes data loss, but executing it too frequently can cause performance issues, so debouncing or adjusting the save timing is necessary. Settings must distinguish between default values and user-modified values, and migration or fallback mechanisms may be required if data from previous versions remains. When reading the code, check the storage keys, JSON parse failure handling, default values, version changes, synchronization conflicts, and deletion flow in that order. The key question is whether the user can safely resume what they were doing. A9_BODY_THICKENED: When reviewing save and restore code, check the save key, default values, handling of parsing failures, and version changes in that order. When storing values in localStorage or other storage systems, they are often stored as strings, so the JSON stringify and parse processes are necessary. Since data saved in previous versions may not be compatible with the new code, fallbacks and migration are also important. Auto-save and debounce ensure that user input is not lost while preventing overly frequent saves. For settings, you must distinguish between values changed by the user and the app’s default values. State restoration is a feature that ensures learning progress, filters, notes, and completion rates are seamlessly carried over when the app is reopened. It’s best to design the system so that, even if restoration fails, it reverts to safe default values.
when_to_show: You can view runtime product features, user status, search and filters, notes, progress, performance, and UI feedback all together on a single card.
detail: Saving and restoring state is a feature that allows users to continue their learning progress even after reopening the app. We’ll look at localStorage, JSON parsing, default values, version changes, migration, fallback, and debounce together. Even if something goes wrong, the app must revert to a safe default, and it must distinguish between settings changed by the user and the default values.

title: Large list performance is evaluated by considering rendering, pagination, and feedback together
body: If there are too many cards, the app may slow down—even if the features work as intended—which can disrupt the learning flow. Whenever terms like pagination, virtual list, large list, rendering, loading indicator, or performance budget come up, check how much content is being displayed on the screen at any given time. Pagination displays data in batches, while virtual lists reduce the cost of handling long lists by rendering only the visible portion. Loading indicators explain the wait time, and performance metrics allow you to compare performance before and after improvements. Performance code isn’t just about appearing fast—it must also work in tandem with filters, search, side card display, and mobile scrolling. When reading the code, consider the number of rendering cycles, list length, caching, user feedback, and empty state handling. A9_BODY_THICKENED: When reading performance code for large lists, you must distinguish between the total number of data points and the number of items actually displayed on the screen. When there are hundreds of cards, rendering all items at once can slow things down. Pagination divides results into pages, while virtual lists save performance by rendering only the area visible on the screen. A loading indicator helps users understand why they are waiting, and the performance budget serves as a benchmark for determining the target speed. When used with search and filters, check whether the entire list is recalculated every time the conditions change or if caching is possible. On mobile, scroll and touch responsiveness are also important. Performance-optimized code isn’t just about speed—it’s about creating a seamless reading experience for the user.

detail: When evaluating the performance of large lists, it is important to distinguish between the total number of data items and the number of items actually rendered on the screen. Pagination and virtual lists are methods for reducing the rendering cost of long lists. When used in conjunction with search and filters, you should also check the cache, loading indicators, and mobile scroll responsiveness. Performance improvements aim not only for speed but also for a seamless user experience.

title: UI flow and feedback help users understand their current status.
body: UI flow and feedback are features that help users understand what is happening when they press a button. When terms such as “loading state,” “empty state,” “error state,” “event handler,” “click,” “feedback,” and “user action” come up, examine how the screen state responds to user actions. A good UI clearly distinguishes between success, failure, waiting, and empty results, and provides options for the next action. In a learning app, submitting the correct answer, changing filters, saving notes, moving cards, and failed API requests are all subjects for feedback. When reading the code, check which events change which states, how those states are represented by text or buttons, and whether there is a recovery flow in case of failure. UI flow is the glue that connects functionality with the user’s understanding. A9_BODY_THICKENED: UI Flow and Feedback When reading code, I connect user actions, state changes, and screen displays in a single thread. Event handlers—such as button clicks or input changes—alter the internal state, and that state is represented on the screen as “loading,” “empty,” “error,” or “success.” A good UI tells users what they clicked, what they are currently waiting for, and what they can do next if an error occurs. In a learning app, submitting the correct answer, moving to the next card, applying filters, saving notes, and data loading failures are all subjects for feedback. Error messages should be guidance that users can understand, not developer logs. When reading the code, check to see if the state names, conditional branches, display text, recovery buttons, and accessibility guidance all work together seamlessly.

detail: UI flow and feedback are read as a single, continuous sequence linking user actions, state changes, and screen displays. Button clicks or changes in input lead to states such as “loading,” “empty,” “error,” or “success.” A good UI lets users know what they’re waiting for and what they can do next if something goes wrong.
